011.headline: Rio's Soapstone Art Deco Colossus Offers Sweeping Bay Views but Zero Sourdough Starter
011.p1: Perched atop the 710-meter granite peak of Corcovado, Christ the Redeemer was first proposed in the 1850s by Vincentian priest Pedro Maria Boss, though nobody funded it until Rio's Catholic archdiocese passed the hat in the 1920s. Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and sculptor Paul Landowski rejected an early sketch showing Christ holding a globe like a bowling ball, settling instead on a thirty-meter reinforced-concrete figure with a twenty-eight-meter armspan. Because concrete cracks in tropical sun, thousands of parish women glued six million tiny triangular tiles of pale Swedish soapstone onto linen sheets, often writing relatives' names on the back before workers cemented them to the statue prior to its October 1931 unveiling.
011.p2: Getting up Corcovado today via the red Swiss cog-wheel train takes twenty minutes of rattling through the Tijuca rainforest, followed by a viewing terrace so densely packed that extending both arms to mimic the statue guarantees slapping two strangers in the face. To capture the mandatory low-angle photograph without forty other tourists' heads in the frame, dozens of people lie flat on their backs on the hot stone pavement around the pedestal, creating a perilous obstacle course of sprawled limbs and expensive camera lenses. About forty percent of the time, a thick Atlantic cloud rolls onto the summit thirty seconds before your train arrives, turning the entire world above Christ's kneecaps into a uniform sheet of wet gray flannel.
011.p3: Even on a clear afternoon, the 635-ton monument failed to rise to the occasion for @CrumbBum, who rode the funicular up Corcovado expecting Crust the Redeemer. In a scathing review titled 'Unleavened Experience!', our carb-focused critic complained that the towering figure offered only 'dry, bland crumbs' and resembled a 'gigantic, stale bread man' overlooking Guanabara Bay. It takes an extraordinary devotion to artisanal baking to ascend two thousand feet up a Brazilian granite pinnacle, inspect six million hand-laid steatite tiles that survive six lightning strikes a year, and deduct four stars because the statue wasn't proofed with active dry yeast and brushed with garlic butter.
011.visitor_tip: Check the live Corcovado summit webcam before buying your cog-train ticket at Cosme Velho station, because once the mountain is wrapped in clouds you won't even see the statue's toes from ten feet away.

012.headline: Rome's Flavian Amphitheatre Boasts Eighty Arched Entrances and Nowhere to Hang a Winter Coat
012.p1: Begun by Emperor Vespasian in 72 AD on the site of Nero's private lake and inaugurated by his son Titus in 80 AD with a hundred-day festival that slaughtered nine thousand wild animals, the Colosseum was funded by war booty looted from Jerusalem. Officially the Flavian Amphitheatre, it picked up the nickname Colosseum in the Middle Ages because it stood beside a thirty-meter bronze statue of Nero that later emperors remodeled into the sun god. After gladiatorial bouts faded, the travertine arena served as a medieval clan fortress, a quarry for St. Peter's, and a wild botanical garden where nineteenth-century English naturalists cataloged 420 species of exotic plants sprouted from seeds dropped by ancient circus beasts.
012.p2: Modern combat occurs outside on the sun-baked cobbled piazza around the Arch of Constantine, where unlicensed promoters dressed as centurions in plastic breastplates and red nylon helmet brushes ambush anyone making eye contact. Even with a pre-booked timed entry ticket, clearing the security gates involves shuffling slowly through two concentric iron cattle-pens before climbing vertical travertine stairs designed for the considerably longer strides of first-century Roman legionaries. Once inside the upper tiers, you peer down into the exposed brick maze of the hypogeum while tour guides in twelve languages wave telescoping umbrellas overhead and explain how hand-cranked wooden capstans and bronze trapdoors hoisted seasick leopards into the midday Italian glare.
012.p3: That subterranean staging area deeply offended @CrampedCrusader, who arrived at the Piazza del Colosseo with an armful of dry cleaning expecting the Closet Museum. Writing under the banner 'Definitely not gladiatorial!', our reviewer complained that the fifty-thousand-seat amphitheatre was 'too cramped for my toga collection' and lacked cedar coat hangers or decent track lighting for displaying old tunics. While thirty-six trapdoors and two miles of underground corridors were admittedly snug for waiting lions and nervous gladiators, criticizing Emperor Vespasian for failing to install a walk-in wardrobe organizer with laminated shoe cubbies is a bold new frontier in classical interior design.
012.visitor_tip: Buy your combined Colosseum, Forum, and Palatine Hill ticket directly on the official Parco Archeologico website thirty days out, and enter the Roman Forum via the quiet Via di San Gregorio gate.

013.headline: Fifty-Mile Isthmian Waterway Relies on Gravity-Fed Concrete Locks Rather Than Flannel Buttons
013.p1: Ferdinand de Lesseps, fresh off his triumph at Suez, launched a French attempt to dig a sea-level canal across Panama in 1881, only to lose twenty-two thousand workers to yellow fever, malaria, and catastrophic Culebra Cut landslides before going bankrupt in 1889. When the United States took over the rusted French steam shovels in 1904, chief sanitary officer Dr. William Gorgas eradicated the mosquito population by fumigating every house and pouring oil on standing puddles, while chief engineer John Frank Stevens convinced Teddy Roosevelt to abandon the sea-level fantasy in favour of damming the Chagres River to create Gatun Lake eighty-five feet above the oceans. Because the isthmus bends like a sleeping snake, ships sailing from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travel from northwest to southeast.
013.p2: Most visitors observe this geopolitical hydraulic feat from the four-story concrete terraces of the Miraflores Visitor Center outside Panama City, where admission includes an IMAX movie narrated in booming baritone by Morgan Freeman. Unless you verify the transit schedule beforehand, you risk spending two hours between 10:30 AM and 2:00 PM staring at an empty concrete bathtub while humid ninety-degree air fogs your sunglasses and a loudspeaker enthusiastically announces the tonnage of a tugboat. When a Neo-Panamax container ship stacked twelve stories high with Maersk boxes finally inches into the lock chamber pulled by electric 'mule' locomotives, eight hundred tourists press against the glass railing and cheer as twenty-six million gallons of lake water drain by gravity in eight minutes.
013.p3: Gravity-fed chambers and electric locomotives brought zero comfort to @ComfyCaptain, who steamed toward Colón expecting a cozy cruise down the Pajama Canal. In 'Definitely NOT a shortcut to dreamland,' our sleep-deprived mariner protested that their vessel wouldn't fit through the 'buttons' and expressed total bewilderment that an international maritime corridor was not tailored from breathable brushed cotton flannel. Considering that the average container ship pays upward of four hundred thousand dollars in tolls just to squeeze through the Culebra Cut with two feet of clearance on either side, demanding elastic waistbands and fleece lapels from the Panama Canal Authority seems optimistic.
013.visitor_tip: Call or check the Miraflores Locks transit schedule before taking a taxi out from Panama City, because container ships only pass through the Pacific locks during specific morning and mid-afternoon tidal windows.

014.headline: Westminster's 13.5-Ton Hour Bell Proves Stubbornly Hostile to Mindfulness and Chakra Alignment
014.p1: As every London cabbie will inform you before the meter hits four pounds, 'Big Ben' is technically the nickname of the 13.5-ton Great Bell inside the belfry, whereas the 96-meter neo-Gothic structure designed by Augustus Pugin is the Elizabeth Tower. Cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry in 1858 after the original sixteen-ton bell cracked during testing in Palace Yard, the replacement developed its own three-foot fissure two months after being hoisted up the shaft because lawyer and amateur horologist Edmund Beckett Denison insisted on fitting a hammer twice the weight recommended by the foundry. Rather than melt it down again, engineers rotated the bell a quarter-turn, filed a square notch to stop the crack spreading, and left Westminster with its famously slightly flat E-natural bong.
014.p2: Admiring Pugin's gilded dial faces after their 80-million-pound conservation scrub usually requires standing on the narrow pavement of Westminster Bridge, an area currently shared by three thousand tourists, four illegal cup-and-ball hustlers, and a man in a Shrek costume charging five pounds for a photograph. Foreign visitors cannot simply buy a ticket to climb the 334 spiral stairs inside the tower on a whim; public tours sell out three months in advance to fast-clicking insiders at 10:00 AM on the second Wednesday of the month. Down on street level, the red double-decker Route 24 bus honks continuously at people stepping backward into the bike lane to frame the clock face behind a red telephone box.
014.p3: That sensory assault completely derailed @NoInnerPeaceNed, who unrolled a foam yoga mat at the corner of Bridge Street and Parliament Square expecting a tranquil retreat at Big Zen. Complaining in 'My Qi is Still Blocked!' that 'incessant bonging ruined my focus' every fifteen minutes, our mindfulness seeker picked the single loudest intersection in British democracy to attempt lotus pose. Expecting a Victorian striking mechanism regulated by stacks of old copper pennies on its thirteen-foot pendulum to hush its four quarter-bells so you can locate your third eye beside the muddy Thames is a charmingly optimistic view of nineteenth-century parliamentary timekeeping.
014.visitor_tip: Walk across Westminster Bridge to the quiet stone embankment wall directly downstairs in front of St. Thomas' Hospital for a clean, crowd-free photo of the Elizabeth Tower and Parliament.

015.headline: Two-Thousand-Kilometer Coral Ecosystem Off Queensland Yields Zero Blueberries or Whipped Cream
015.p1: Stretching 2,300 kilometers along the Queensland continental shelf from the Torres Strait to Lady Elliot Island, the Great Barrier Reef is not a single wall of rock but an archipelago of roughly 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands built over half a million years by billions of tiny coral polyps secreting calcium carbonate skeletons. Its European discovery was markedly less than serene: on the night of June 11, 1770, Lieutenant James Cook's HMS Endeavour slammed straight into a submerged coral outcrop later named Endeavour Reef, forcing his crew to heave six iron cannons and forty tons of ballast overboard before fothering the hole with a sail stuffed with sheep's wool and dung to limp ashore at Cooktown.
015.p2: Modern explorers generally depart from the Cairns marina at 8:00 AM aboard high-speed aluminum catamarans carrying two hundred passengers, sixty percent of whom spend the ninety-minute outer-reef crossing discovering that the Coral Sea swell does not respect hotel buffet breakfasts. Upon mooring at a floating steel pontoon, everyone is zipped into head-to-toe black Lycra stinger suits to ward off translucent irukandji jellyfish the size of a thumbnail, transforming a boatload of holidaymakers into a squad of middle-aged scuba ninjas. Once in the water, you spend forty minutes accidentally kicking someone else's neon-yellow flipper while breathing through a plastic tube and watching a four-foot Maori wrasse stare back at you with profound fish indifference.
015.p3: Even the giant clams and neon parrotfish failed to sweeten the mood for @BerryBlue, who paddled off the Cairns pontoon expecting the Great Berry Reef. In a tearful one-star critique titled 'More like Great Berry GRIEF!', our reviewer complained of seeing 'more jellyfish than blueberries down under' and lamented the total absence of raspberries, boysenberries, or a floating fruit-salad bar in the Coral Sea. Swimming forty miles offshore into 344,000 square kilometers of saltwater marine park with a dessert spoon tucked into your wetsuit sleeve is an unforgettable way to learn the difference between anthozoan cnidarians and the grocery store produce aisle.
015.visitor_tip: If you get seasick on open-ocean catamarans, book a smaller sailboat trip to the Low Isles from Port Douglas or fly down to Lady Musgrave Island on the southern reef where the lagoon is calm as a bath.

016.headline: Wyoming's Supervolcano Caldera Erupts on Schedule Without Assistance From a Blacksmith's Forge
016.p1: Established by President Ulysses S. Grant in March 1872 as the world's first national park, Yellowstone sits directly atop a restless forty-five-mile-wide volcanic caldera that has blown its lid three times in the past 2.1 million years. When fur trapper John Colter walked out of the Tetons in 1807 describing boiling mud pots, petrified forests, and sulfurous steam vents, polite easterners laughed it off as 'Colter's Hell' and assumed mountain fever had cooked his brain. Today the park's 2.2 million acres contain half of the planet's active geothermal features, including roughly five hundred geysers fed by snowmelt seeping miles down into rhyolite rock heated by a magma chamber resting just three miles beneath the tourists' hiking sandals.
016.p2: Experiencing this untamed wilderness in July mostly consists of sitting motionless in a rented SUV for ninety minutes because a single grumpy bull bison has decided to use the northbound lane of the Grand Loop Road as a back-scratcher. At Old Faithful, three thousand people line a semi-circular wooden bench thirty minutes before the predicted eruption window, staring intently at a steaming gravel mound in a silence usually reserved for golf putts. Over at Grand Prismatic Spring, gusts of sulfur-scented steam routinely snatch baseball caps off heads and deposit them onto fragile orange bacterial mats, where they remain alongside decades of sunglasses because stepping off the wooden boardwalk carries a mandatory federal court appearance.
016.p3: Hydrothermal plumbing held zero charm for @WindbagWanderer, who drove across the Wyoming basin expecting Bellowstone National Park. Under the headline 'A Resounding Disappointment,' our reviewer griped that the Continental Divide contained 'just a bunch of noisy huffing and puffing' without a single leather blacksmith's bellows in sight, adding that the steam gusts rendered their yellow raincoat useless. One has to salute the determination of a traveler who drives past four thousand bison and ten thousand fumaroles looking for a giant fireplace air-pump, only to fault a supervolcano for operating via subterranean water pressure rather than two hinged wooden paddles and a brass nozzle.
016.visitor_tip: Skip the crowded ground-level boardwalk at Grand Prismatic Spring until midday when the morning steam clears, and hike the short Fairy Falls trail overlook for the famous aerial view of the rainbow rings.

017.headline: Tuscany's Tilted Romanesque Bell Tower Remains Stubbornly Unhelpful With the Kitchen Mop
017.p1: Begun in August 1173 as the freestanding campanile for Pisa's cathedral, the tower made it to the third story in 1178 before its architect, probably Bonanno Pisano, noticed that three meters of shallow foundation set in waterlogged clay and sea-sand was sinking on the south side. Fortunately for physics, Pisa spent the next century picking fights with Genoa, Lucca, and Florence, halting construction for nearly a hundred years and allowing the underlying soil to compress under the weight; had they finished on schedule, the tower would have toppled straight into the piazza. When Giovanni di Simone resumed work in 1272, he tried to compensate by building the upper floors taller on the downhill side, giving the 56-meter marble cylinder the subtle curve of a petrified banana.
017.p2: Step through the Porta Santa Maria onto the Piazza dei Miracoli at 11:00 AM and you are greeted by the surreal sight of five hundred adults standing on the walkway with both hands raised in the air like silent-film mimes trapped in an invisible box. From every side angle, the lawn resembles a mass tai-chi class in which strangers take turns pretending to prop up, kick over, or balance the twelfth-century marble tower inside an ice-cream cone. If you pay twenty euros to climb the 251 internal steps, the 3.97-degree tilt creates the unsettling nautical sensation of walking up a spiral staircase during a force-eight gale, tossing you gently from the inner wall to the outer wall on every half turn.
017.p3: That gravitational lurch only compounded the misery for @SudsSufferer, who arrived in Tuscany armed with rubber gloves and a bucket expecting the Cleaning Tower of Pisa. In 'Seriously Misleading Name!', our tidy critic complained that there was 'not one mop in all of Tuscany' inside the monument and that the pronounced tilt made it impossible to scrub the worn marble floors without getting dizzy. After Italian engineers spent thirty million euros between 1990 and 2001 extracting thirty-eight cubic meters of dirt to keep the tower from collapsing, it feels harsh to dock them four stars for not stocking lemon-scented Pine-Sol in the belfry.
017.visitor_tip: Don't leave after ten minutes like the tour bus crowds; walk five minutes south to Piazza dei Cavalieri to see Vasari's sgraffito facades without a single person miming a karate chop in the air.

018.headline: Midtown Manhattan's 102-Story Art Deco Skyscraper Contains Zero Velvet Coffins in the Basement
018.p1: Constructed during the depths of the Great Depression in an astonishing 410 days, the Empire State Building rose at a pace of four and a half stories per week as 3,400 Mohawk ironworkers and European immigrant riveters bolted together 57,000 tons of Pittsburgh steel. Financiers John Jakob Raskob and Al Smith topped the 381-meter tower with a 61-meter mooring mast intended for transatlantic dirigibles, where passengers were supposed to stroll down an open gangplank 1,250 feet above Fifth Avenue; the scheme was quietly abandoned after a Navy airship tried docking in forty-mile-per-hour updrafts in 1931 and nearly stood on its nose. Because so few tenants could afford offices in 1931, wags nicknamed it the 'Empty State Building,' and observation-deck ticket sales alone kept the lights on.
018.p2: Reaching the 86th-floor open-air observation deck today requires surviving a forty-five-minute indoor labyrinth on the second floor that winds past museum exhibits about nineties rom-coms, a giant robotic King Kong hand poking through fake office plaster, and three separate mandatory green-screen photo booths where staff attempt to sell you a thirty-five-dollar souvenir print of yourself looking tired in front of a fake skyline. Two express elevator rides later, you step out onto the wrap-around terrace behind steel suicide-fence bars, jostling for six inches of parapet space in a biting Hudson River crosswind while listening to a heavy coin-operated steel binocular click shut just before you focus on the Chrysler Building.
018.p3: Bright fluorescent lobby lighting and daylight views were a mortal insult to @NightCrawlerNY, who crept onto West 34th Street after midnight expecting the Vampire State Building. Firing off a one-star review titled 'Fang-tastic...ly Awful!', our nocturnal visitor complained that the elevators went to the 86th floor instead of a damp Carpathian crypt, and noted with disgust that the Art Deco brass restrooms were full of mirrors. Admittedly, Manhattan commercial real estate has drawn plenty of bloodsuckers since 1931, but blaming architects Shreve, Lamb & Harmon for failing to install gargoyle perches and O-negative juice bars on the 102nd floor seems slightly unfair.
018.visitor_tip: Skip the extra thirty-dollar upcharge for the cramped, glassed-in 102nd floor and stick to the open-air 86th-floor deck after 10:00 PM when the tour groups thin out.

019.headline: Manhattan's Neon Crossroads Delivers Four Hundred Million Pedestrians and Zero Fresh Citrus
019.p1: Until April 1904, the bow-tie intersection where Broadway slices across Seventh Avenue was known as Longacre Square, a gritty district of carriage factories, horse stables, and blacksmith shops presided over by William H. Vanderbilt's American Horse Exchange. Everything changed when publisher Adolph Ochs moved the headquarters of The New York Times into a narrow twenty-five-story neo-Gothic tower at 42nd Street and persuaded Mayor George B. McClellan Jr. to rename the subway station and the plaza in his newspaper's honor. Ochs celebrated New Year's Eve that December with fireworks from the roof, switching in 1907 to a seven-hundred-pound iron-and-wood ball covered in a hundred twenty-five-watt lightbulbs after city officials banned his pyrotechnics for raining hot cinders onto theatergoers' hats.
019.p2: The newspaper moved out of One Times Square in 1913 and the building stands almost entirely empty today because it makes far more money as a 360-foot pole for fifty-million-dollar LED billboards. Crossing Duffy Square at 8:00 PM means swimming through 360,000 bewildered pedestrians under light so bright it is visible from the International Space Station, while dodging five separate unlicensed performers in flea-bitten Elmo suits, two Iron Mans with sagging foam abs, and aggressive guys trying to hand you a 'free' hip-hop CD before demanding twenty dollars once you touch the plastic case. Native New Yorkers will walk four avenues out of their way in pouring rain rather than set foot between 42nd and 47th Streets.
019.p3: Not even the three-story M&M's World store could rescue the evening for @SourPuss, who emerged from the N-Q-R subway stairs with a cocktail shaker expecting Limes Square. Writing in 'A Real Squeeze!', our scurvy-conscious critic lamented the total absence of tart green citrus trees on the red fiberglass TKTS steps and complained that forty-story high-definition advertisements for Broadway musicals contain zero daily value of Vitamin C. While spending forty-five minutes trapped behind slow-walking tourists outside the Olive Garden on 47th Street will certainly leave a sour taste in anyone's mouth, expecting Midtown asphalt to garnish a margarita is a tall order.
019.visitor_tip: If you must pass through Times Square, walk strictly along the painted pedestrian plazas in the center of Broadway rather than the choked sidewalks, and never accept anything handed to you by a plush cartoon character.

020.headline: Dubai's Half-Mile Steel-and-Glass Needle Serves Expensive Gold-Leaf Coffee Instead of Drive-Thru Patties
020.p1: Designed by Chicago skyscraper veteran Adrian Smith of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill using a three-lobed buttressed footprint inspired by the desert spider lily, the Burj Khalifa tops out at 828 meters and 163 habitable floors, more than twice the height of the Empire State Building. Known as the Burj Dubai during its six-year construction, the tower was abruptly renamed on opening night in January 2010 to honor Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan, ruler of neighboring Abu Dhabi, who had discreetly wired ten billion dollars days earlier to bail out Dubai World's debt crisis. Its exterior is clad in 26,000 hand-cut glass panels that take thirty-six window washers on mechanized cradles three full months to squeegee from top to bottom.
020.p2: You cannot simply walk through a front door off the street; reaching the 'At the Top' elevators requires hiking a mile through the subterranean levels of the Dubai Mall past an indoor shark aquarium, an Olympic ice rink, and four hundred luxury handbag boutiques. Even with a pre-booked sixty-dollar ticket for the 124th floor, you will spend up to an hour snaking through velvet ropes before a double-deck elevator shoots you skyward at ten meters per second while projections of other buildings you are passing flash on the walls. Stepping onto the outdoor terrace at 452 meters, you peer through narrow vertical slots in the glass wall into a hundred-degree desert haze that makes the Persian Gulf look like warm milk.
020.p3: All that structural engineering left an empty stomach for @GreasyGastronaut, who rode the elevator 124 floors into the Arabian sky expecting the Burger Khalifa. In 'More Grease Than Glamour!', our fast-food pilgrim complained that their 'towering desert dream crumbled like stale sesame buns' and expressed shock that the observation deck wasn't slathered in secret special sauce or stacked with charbroiled beef patties. Paying fifty-five dirhams at the summit cafe for a cappuccino dusted with twenty-four-karat edible gold leaf is undeniably steep, but blaming the world's tallest freestanding structure for not coming with crinkle-cut fries and a pickle spear is a high-altitude misunderstanding.
020.visitor_tip: Instead of paying extra for the crowded 148th-floor observation deck, book a table with a window minimum spend at Atmosphere on the 122nd floor for roughly the same price and an actual drink in your hand.
